en: If you give me your fine-cloth robe, I shall wear it;
Give me Buurul and let me ride him.
I shall learn who belongs to the caravan
Where thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens
Are playing.
Radiant like the younger son of Manas,
Let me shine
And walk among them as a man."
When he asked for Buurul,
The tiger did not grow sorrowful.
Unable to say, "I will not give him,"
He did not turn back his hero's heart;
Unable to say, "Stop, young man,"
He did not reject the first desire
Of the poor man born alone.
The tiger born to surpass
His father, gray-wolf Manas, said:
"If you would wear it, put it on,"
And took off and gave him the fine-cloth robe.
"If you would ride him, mount him,"
And dismounted and gave him Buurul.
Once the words "I give him" left his mouth,
Would your heroic companion stand still?
He sprang up and ran,
And seized the bridle
Of Buurul, standing in the line.
Tall, lean Buurul had come into condition;
The poor beast stood there restlessly.
His elder had traveled this way,
And sweated out the horse's bitter sweat.
He had removed the saddle and left him bare,
And placed him in the yellow breeze;
Through this the sleek horse
Had returned to fighting condition.
The bow-shaped wretch's
Mane and tail had grown thin;
He bristled as he came into condition,
And assumed an altered form.
Gazing ceaselessly at the sky,
Every joint and bone
Drew smilingly into his frame.
He raced with flying birds
And wrestled whoever held him.
The belly flesh from which kazy is taken
Had remained drawn tightly inward,
Clinging against his ribs.
Snorting and darting about,
The sleek horse played,
And with his muzzle tossed the young man
Like a skullcap through the air.
Semetey, the hero none could stir,
The hero born to surpass his father, said:
"Hey, hey, what is the swine doing?
His vigor has returned to his flesh;
This is the hour his ardor has risen."
Your young lord strode forward
And approached the courser.
Standing tall, he caught him himself;
He held the courser firmly,
Not allowing him to move.
Kulchoro came and saddled the horse;
With remarkable quickness
He saddled him in a flash.
A leather saddlecloth and blue pad
He laid straight upon his back;
The Akkangky made by Almambet,
A saddle fitted for Semetey,
Its front bow of white gold,
And its rear bow entirely of silver,
Both saddle bows were broad iron;
It would not shift when ridden in wrestling,
So skillfully was Akkangky made.
He shortened the crupper,
Lengthened the girth,
Drew the flank strap tight,
And lengthened the breast strap.
Kulchoro asked his elder
For the noble courser;
As soon as his elder gave it,
Without setting foot in the gold-soled stirrup,
Onto the noble courser
He vaulted in a single leap.
Would that hot-blooded young man stand still?
Once he had put on the fine-cloth robe,
Once he had mounted Buurul,
The sight opened the heart:
Gray-wolf Kulchoro
Looked like Semetey.
When the young man began to ride away,
His elder waved his hand and shouted;
Your poor lord called after him:
"Listen carefully to my words.
Lest your eyes become blind,
I had you made into a mullah.
You have the learning to read a lesson;
Buurul is my own wing.
Keep him reined on stony ground;
If you meet her on the open plain,
Give greetings and blessings
To Churok, daughter of Akun.
Do not behave like a heedless youth, my dear one;
If you see a raven, do not chase it.
The poor beast is in the fullness of condition—
May he not plunge a foot into a pit
And fail to pull his leg free.
Amid thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens,
With Aychurok in their midst,
May he not go lumbering awkwardly;
May they not mock you, saying,
'The poor man's horse is lame.'
Be wary of this.
You were always reckless, Kulchoro;
This is a thoroughbred courser.
If you see a crow, do not chase it;
May tall Buurul beneath you,
Sparing nothing of his poor life,
Not break into a headlong run,
Set his foot in a hollow,
And fail to pull it free.
May he not approach the maidens at the ford
Limping with a haughty air;
May the maidens and daughters-in-law there
Not mock you, saying,
'It is the lame horse of that poor fellow.'
My only one whom I have cradled,
I have given you Akolpok; wear it there.
I have given you the tall courser; ride him there.
If six divisions of black enemies appear,
Try striking the foe without flinching;
Understand: this is what I tell you.
Many enemies will lose heart,
And many foes will come over the land;
There are many hills that harbor thieves,
And many enemies lying in wait,
Many places with towering cliffs,
And many heroes ready to fight.
If you are delayed, it will bring disgrace;
Buurul the horse is entrusted to you!
You are only a boy of twelve;
Do not begin an uproar.
I have no horse beneath me,
And no coat upon me;
Do not leave your elder and lord
Stranded in this place!
Go swiftly, my Kulchoro,
Scout the city of Akun,
And from your poor sister-in-law Aychurok
Ask for Akshunkar and bring it back!
If you abandon it, there will be disgrace;
From your poor, fortunate sister-in-law
I entrust you to ask for the white falcon!"
While Semetey stood speaking,
The young man shot away without stopping;
From beside Semetey,
Before one could say this or that,
He vanished from sight.
He urged Buurul in surging strides;
Without turning back, Kulchoro
Drove him as wildly as one bereaved.
Before one could say this or that,
In the time it took to open and close one's eyes,
Hero Choro, sustained by Saint Shay,
Had crossed over
The pass of Agynek at speed.
Like a practiced horseman,
He covered Buurul beneath him
With a broadcloth horse-cover.
Behold the wonder of the young man:
He rode red Buurul.
Distinctive was Buurul's nature;
He tied the horsehair tail in a firm knot.
Semetey's tall Buurul
Had grown fat upon tumbleweed grass;
His sleekness was like a lance,
And that creature Buurul
Jumped like a flea.
The sight made the viewer's soul burn;
His splendid, abundant forelock
Seemed tied precisely level with his eyes.
His splayed hind legs were like a ravine;
The white blaze upon his forehead
Was like steel tempered and set.
His great hooves were broad as basins,
And the croup behind him
Was like an open, unbounded plain.
No mother could say, "I bore him here,"
And no father could say, "I sired him."
He was a child of the wind spirit,
A racer alongside the wild kulan,
Born of Tulpar
And Maid Saykal's Algara.
He did not start when he heard an uproar;
Even amid shots that deafened the ear,
He never misplaced a single step.
Raised apart among the spirits,
This creature, the horse Buurul,
Grew upon rocks where deer could not walk.
He skimmed across mountain summits,
Leading ninety swift horses,
And roamed across countless lands.
He summered with the spirits
And grappled with wild kulan.
Ask nothing of every limb
Of Buurul standing in the line.
Ridden for six months, he would not tire;
Driven over hills, he would not wear down.
Until he reached sixty years of age,
His molars would not loosen with age.
Saying, "He may flee the saddle,"
They made him drag a rope from his neck;
Saying, "His limbs will become bronze,"
They trained him over rolling ground.
When Buurul was a yearling,
They had an amulet fixed around his neck;
The horse-judges tested and approved him.
Fondling him, hero Manas
Had him fed from the treasury's stores.
Long ago an owl feather was fastened to his head.
When Buurul belonged to Manas,
He curved his neck like a deer;
If game a target's height appeared,
He leaped without hesitation.
Once his quality as a courser was known,
Offering weighed gold and fine cloth,
The khan of Bukhara asked for him.
Manas did not give him to those who asked;
Far from giving Buurul away,
He let no ritually impure person ride him.
He curved his neck like an argali;
If game a rope-length high appeared,
He leaped without fail.
Once his heroic quality was known,
Offering white ingots and costly cloth,
Khans from every land asked for him.
Unlike every other beast,
Buurul possessed wings;
Which of his feats shall we tell?
If the road was forty days long,
He would not so much as sip water;
If there was a dangerous deep pit,
He never stepped astray and fell.
Kulchoro drove Buurul standing in the line,
Making him leap with a roar.
God creates every living soul;
That young man Kulchoro
Was traveling onward to Urgench.
Kulchoro hurried breathlessly;
Early words seemed late,
So eager was he to arrive early,
Watching with all four eyes.
When he came out upon the pass,
Ask nothing of the hero's bearing.
Toward spirit-like Buurul,
The black-jawed white whip
He took up and swung;
Kulchoro made it ring aloud,
